Newton's law of universal gravitation (F=−GMmr/∣r∣3)

 Home Physics Branches of physics Classical mechanics
OurBigBook.com Words: 8k Articles: 79
Newton's law of universal gravitation gives the attractive force between two point masses. With source mass M at the origin and relative position r of mass m, write r=∣r∣>0:
FM→m​=−r3GMm​r,∣FM→m​∣=r2GMm​.
(1)
Here G is the gravitational constant. The minus sign points toward M; the magnitude follows an inverse-square law, so doubling the separation quarters the force. The opposite force on M satisfies Newton's third law. [ref]
Both masses accelerate. Applying Newton's second law to each in the isolated two-body problem gives
r¨=−r3μ​r,μ=G(M+m).
(2)
The relative standard gravitational parameter includes both masses; replacing it by GM requires the test particle approximation m≪M.
Historically, Newton's Book III, Proposition VII argues that gravitational attraction applies to all bodies and scales with their masses; its second corollary states the inverse-square law for individual particles. [ref]

Axial and transverse gravity of a uniform rod (F∥​=GMm/(b2−a2),F⊥​=GMm/[rr2+a2​])

Newton's law of universal gravitation OurBigBook.com
Integrate Newtonian point-force elements along a uniform thin rod of total mass M and half-length a. The first title formula applies on the axis outside the endpoint, b>a; the second applies on its perpendicular bisector. Both approach the point-mass result at large distance, but at equal distance their ratio is 1+3a2/(2b2)+O(a4/b4). A nonuniform linear mass profile cannot be replaced by these formulas using only total mass and length.

Axial and transverse gravity of a uniform rod OurBigBook.com
For a light test mass in the rod's perpendicular-bisector plane, axial symmetry makes the attraction radial. Equating mv2/r to the transverse force gives the title speed. Far outside the rod it is Keplerian, proportional to r−1/2. Well inside the half-length but outside its physical thickness, the rod approximates an infinite line and the circular speed is nearly constant, GM/a​. Extrapolation to an orbit inside the material or a zero-radius orbit is outside this thin-rod model.

Gravitational-electrostatic balance of equal charged spheres (q2/(4πϵ0​)=GM2)

Newton's law of universal gravitation OurBigBook.com
For two identical spheres sufficiently far apart, Coulomb's law and Newton's law of universal gravitation both give inverse-square forces. Equal-sign charges therefore balance attraction when the displayed charge-to-mass relation holds. For uniform mass density ρ, substituting M=4πρa3/3 fixes the radius. Changing the separation does not restore balance if the charge-to-mass ratio is wrong. Spherically symmetric charge makes the monopole result exact outside each sphere; polarization can require a far-field approximation.

Free fall

Words: 863 Articles: 5
Newton's law of universal gravitation OurBigBook.com
Free fall is motion under gravity alone: there is no supporting normal force, engine thrust or appreciable drag force. In the Newtonian mechanics model, a test particle of mass m obeys mr¨=mg(r), hence r¨=g(r). The mass cancels. Bodies released at the same position with the same velocity follow the same path in this model, even if their gravitational weights differ. [ref]
A dropped stone is one example; a coasting satellite is another. Free fall does not require motion straight down or decreasing distance to the attracting body. An ideal circular orbit has constant radius while its velocity continually turns under centripetal acceleration. The circular orbit as continuous free fall connects the familiar drop with orbital motion.
Near a surface, treating the gravitational acceleration as constant gives a useful first prediction. Over larger heights, the inverse-square law changes the acceleration during the fall. Radial free fall from rest uses conservation of mechanical energy to account for that change exactly, within the specified Newtonian gravitational field. The contrast matters: the simplest formula is an approximation to a physical model, rather than a law with the same numerical g everywhere.
History also makes the idealization tangible. Galileo's Two New Sciences (1638), Third Day, Theorem II, derives distance proportional to the square of time for uniformly accelerated motion from rest; its first corollary gives successive distances in the ratios 1,3,5,7,… over equal time intervals. This is a kinematic statement, predating the gravitational inverse-square law. [ref]
On Apollo 15's final lunar surface excursion, David Scott released a hammer and a feather together. The near-vacuum removed the large difference in drag force familiar on Earth. NASA's report describes their arrival together within the accuracy of the release; this demonstration illustrates the free fall prediction without establishing infinite experimental precision. [ref]

Free fall in a constant gravitational field (s(t)=21​gt2,v(t)=gt)

Words: 178
Free fall OurBigBook.com
Take downward displacement s as positive, assume a constant gravitational acceleration g>0, and release a point mass from rest at s=0. Integrating s¨=g twice gives
v(t)=gt,s(t)=21​gt2.
(3)
For a downward distance h>0, the arrival time and speed are
tfall​=g2h​​,varrival​=2gh​.
(4)
For the model values h=20m and g=9.81ms−2, these are approximately 2.0193s and 19.8091ms−1. Doubling the height multiplies both quantities by 2​; it does not double them. The same speed follows from the work-energy theorem, mgh=mv2/2.
For intervals of length Δt, the successive downward displacements are
s((j+1)Δt)−s(jΔt)=21​g(Δt)2(2j+1),j=0,1,2,….
(5)
Thus equal spacing in time produces increasingly separated positions. This is the odd-number pattern in Galileo's result. It assumes constant acceleration and release from rest; a nonzero initial velocity adds a linear term to s(t).
The approximation can be estimated for a spherical source of radius R and standard gravitational parameter μ. Writing g0​=μ/R2, the gravitational magnitude at height h is
g0​g(R+h)​=(1+Rh​)−2.
(6)
For h/R≪1, a Taylor expansion gives g(R+h)/g0​=1−2h/R+O((h/R)2). Small height relative to the source's radius makes nearly constant gravity plausible; negligible drag force remains a separate requirement.

Radial free fall from rest (v(r)=2μ(1/r−1/r0​)​)

Words: 238
Free fall OurBigBook.com
Let a test particle start at rest at radius r0​ outside a fixed spherically symmetric source. The spherical shell theorem gives the exterior Newtonian gravitational potential Φ(r)=−μ/r, where μ=GM is the source's standard gravitational parameter. Zero initial transverse velocity makes the motion radial. Conservation of mechanical energy per unit mass gives
2r˙2​−rμ​=−r0​μ​,r˙=−2μ(r1​−r0​1​)​.
(7)
The minus sign selects inward motion; the positive square root is its speed. For a fall from r0​=2R to the surface r=R, that speed is μ/R​. In the limit of release from rest infinitely far away, the familiar free-fall speed is 2μ/r​, equal in magnitude to the local escape velocity. A finite starting radius gives a smaller speed.
The arrival time follows from the same first integral. Set r=r0​cos2η. Then
t(η)=2μr03​​​(η+sinηcosη),η=arccosr0​r​​,0≤η<2π​.
(8)
For arrival at R>0 this is finite, and the field formula is used only outside the source. For r0​=2R, η=π/4 gives
tarrival​=(1+2π​)μR3​​≈2.570796μR3​​.
(9)
Keeping the smaller initial gravitational magnitude g(r0​)=μ/(4R2) constant would predict 8​R3/μ​, about 10.0% longer. The actual acceleration increases during the fall.
The curves compare a shallow fall, h/R=0.02, with a fall from r0​=2R, so h/R=1. Each comparison holds the release height and initial gravitational magnitude fixed. The constant-gravity model is close for the shallow fall and increasingly inaccurate for the larger one. This is also a practical use of nondimensionalization: the normalized trajectories depend on h/R, while R3/μ​ supplies the dimensional time scale.

Rotational deflection of a falling body

Words: 114 Articles: 1
Free fall OurBigBook.com
In an Earth-fixed rotating reference frame, the horizontal displacement of a freely falling body receives contributions from Coriolis acceleration and centrifugal acceleration. A short-fall approximation substitutes the unperturbed downward velocity into the Coriolis term and the Earth's surface position into the centrifugal term. If gravitational acceleration excludes centrifugal acceleration, both contributions must be included explicitly.

Equatorial Coriolis deflection in free fall (xE​=ΩE​(2h)3/2/(3g​))

Rotational deflection of a falling body OurBigBook.com
A body released from rest relative to Earth at the equator has unperturbed downward velocity vU​=−gt. The Coriolis acceleration in local Earth coordinates gives eastward acceleration aE​=−2ΩE​vU​=2ΩE​gt. Integration gives xE​=ΩE​gt3/3 and impact time tf​=2h/g​, proving the title formula. This is first order in Earth's rotation, neglecting air resistance and the height dependence of the effective local gravitational acceleration. For a short fall at latitude φ, its leading eastward term is multiplied by cosφ.

Newtonian gravitational field (g)

Words: 7k Articles: 69
Newton's law of universal gravitation OurBigBook.com
The Newtonian gravitational field is the gravitational force per unit mass of a test particle. For a point mass M at the origin,
g(r)=mF​=−r3GM​r,g(r)=∣g∣=r2GM​.
(10)
The test particle's mass cancels: different small masses have the same gravitational acceleration at the same position. In SI, the Newtonian gravitational field has units Nkg−1=ms−2. The same exterior expression holds for a spherically symmetric source, by the spherical shell theorem.
Choose a reference radius r0​>0, set g0​=GM/r02​, and use nondimensionalization with z=r/r0​. Then g/g0​=z−2: at z=1,2,4, the magnitudes are 1,1/4,1/16. This makes the spatial variation visible without specifying a planet. [ref]

Gravitational field null between two point masses (x=D/(1+M2​/M1​​))

Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
Two positive point masses M1​,M2​ separated by D have a unique intervening gravitational field zero. At distance x from M1​, Newton's law of universal gravitation gives M1​/x2=M2​/(D−x)2, hence the displayed value. The signed offset towards M2​ from their centre of mass is x−DM2​/(M1​+M2​). This instantaneous cancellation is distinct from a Lagrange point, which includes the centrifugal force of a co-rotating description. Along the joining line the zero is unstable: the derivative of the signed acceleration is 2GM1​/x3+2GM2​/(D−x)3>0.

gr​=−Gλr∫−aa​(r2+z2)3/2dz​=−rr2+a2​GM​.

Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
The outward flux of the Newtonian gravitational field through a closed surface is −4πG times the enclosed mass. A symmetric Gaussian surface can turn the flux relation into a local field calculation, but the integral law alone does not imply that the field is uniform on an arbitrary surface.

Remove a spherical void centered at c from a uniform sphere centered at the origin. At points inside the void, superposition combines the sphere's interior field −4πGρx/3 with the removed sphere's field +4πGρ(x−c)/3. Their sum is the displayed constant Newtonian gravitational field. A second removed mass outside this void adds a nonuniform contribution.

Cavity equilibrium destabilized by a second void

Words: 61
Uniform gravitational field in an off-center spherical cavity OurBigBook.com
A uniform Newtonian gravitational field inside one spherical void can be cancelled at a point by the repulsive field representing another removed sphere. The latter field has a Jacobian matrix proportional to I−3r^r^T: its axial eigenvalue is negative and both transverse eigenvalues positive. The equilibrium is restoring along the axis but unstable transversely. A zero force is thus not enough for stable rest.

Newtonian gravitational stress tensor (Tij​)

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
For a Newtonian gravitational potential obeying the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity, define Tij​=[∂i​Φ∂j​Φ−δij​∣∇Φ∣2/2]/(4πG). Commutation of mixed partial derivatives gives ∂j​Tij​=ρ∂i​Φ. Thus the gravitational force density can be put in conservative form as −∂j​Tij​. The sign is chosen so that Tij​ is added to the momentum flux; reversing the stress convention reverses the divergence sign.

Newtonian gravitational stress tensor OurBigBook.com
In cylindrical coordinates, the Newtonian gravitational stress tensor gives radial angular-momentum flux rTrϕ​=r(∂r​Φ)(r−1∂ϕ​Φ)/(4πG). The isotropic negative-pressure part has zero off-diagonal component, so it gives no direct radial transport. This separates a shear flux from a contribution to normal force balance.

Self-gravity

Words: 35
Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
Self-gravity is the gravitational acceleration produced by a system's own mass density. It is obtained by solving the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity for that density, rather than treating the Newtonian gravitational potential as an externally fixed field. It competes with pressure and rotational support in gravitational instability of an astrophysical disk.

Standard gravitational parameter (μ)

Words: 118
Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
The product μ=GM of the gravitational constant and a central mass sets the strength of the exterior Newtonian gravitational field. Its dimensions are length cubed divided by time squared. In the exact relative two-body problem, the parameter is G(M1​+M2​); using GM for one source assumes the test particle approximation.
The combination is useful because orbital and falling-body observations constrain μ directly. A gravitational circular orbit of radius a has oscillation period T=2πa3/μ​, so measuring a and T gives μ=4π2a3/T2. That measurement alone does not separately determine G and M. Similarly, radial free fall from rest has a natural time scale r03​/μ​.
Other interactions require a different model. Inverse-square radiation pressure can reduce the effective attraction for a dust Kepler orbit; calling that effective coefficient a gravitational parameter must not hide the added force.

Tidal tensor (Tjk​)

Words: 2k Articles: 19
Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
The acceleration tidal tensor is Tjk​=∂k​gj​=−∂j​∂k​Φ for gravitational acceleration g=−∇Φ. It describes differential acceleration Δg≃TΔr. Some authors instead call the positive Hessian matrix ∂j​∂k​Φ the tidal tensor, reversing this sign convention. For a point mass and the positive potential convention g=∇ψ, the tensor is Gm(3RRT/R5−1/R3).
The tidal tensor is the Jacobian matrix of the Newtonian gravitational field, rather than the gravitational acceleration itself. Its entries have units s−2: multiplying by a displacement produces an acceleration. For a smooth Newtonian gravitational potential, the tidal tensor is a symmetric matrix, since mixed partial derivatives commute. A spatially uniform gravitational acceleration has zero tidal tensor, however large that acceleration is.

Surface tidal time scale of a spherical gravitating body (ttide​=R/g​=R3/(GM)​)

Words: 88
Tidal tensor OurBigBook.com
At radius R outside a spherical mass M, the Newtonian relative-acceleration tensor has eigenvalues −g/R,−g/R,2g/R with g=GM/R2. It compresses free fall separations tangentially and stretches them radially. The displayed time scale is the inverse square root of the curvature scale controlling this tidal evolution. An ideal circular orbit at that radius has period 2πttide​, providing a second physical interpretation. For Earth's surface it is about 806 seconds, while the corresponding ideal low-orbit period is about 84 minutes. A uniform gravitational acceleration does not determine this relative motion; spatial variation of the field does.

Corotating point-mass tidal field (Teff​=Ω2diag(3,0,−1))

Words: 72
Tidal tensor OurBigBook.com
Use local axes radial, tangential in the orbital plane, and perpendicular to that plane around a circular Kepler orbit with Ω2=GM/R3. The gravitational tidal tensor is Ω2diag(2,−1,−1). A uniformly corotating frame adds the gradient of centrifugal acceleration, Ω2diag(1,1,0), giving the displayed effective tensor for stationary offsets. Thus the radial differential acceleration is 3GMa/R3. These are accelerations, or forces per unit test mass; an actual differential force includes that mass. Moving offsets also experience Coriolis acceleration.

Point-mass tidal stretching and squeezing (T=μ(3nnT−I)/R3)

Words: 174
Tidal tensor OurBigBook.com
For a source point mass M at the origin, let R=Rn, where n is an outward unit vector, and let μ=GM be the source's standard gravitational parameter. Differentiating gi​=−μRi​/R3 gives the tidal tensor
Tij​=R3μ​(3ni​nj​−δij​),T=R3μ​(3nnT−I),
(13)
where δij​ is the Kronecker delta and I is the identity matrix. In an orthonormal basis with first axis radial, the tidal tensor is
T=R3μ​​200​0−10​00−1​​.
(14)
The radial eigenvalue 2μ/R3 separates nearby freely falling test particles; the two transverse eigenvalues −μ/R3 bring them together. The farther radial test particle falls inward less rapidly, so its acceleration relative to the nearer one points outward. Transverse gravitational accelerations converge toward the source. Thus an initially resting small cloud stretches radially and squeezes in both transverse directions. These are instantaneous relative accelerations; the subsequent shape also depends on initial velocities and the changing tidal tensor along the cloud's free fall.
Outside the source, the matrix trace is 2μ/R3−μ/R3−μ/R3=0. This matches trT=−∇2Φ=0 in a region with zero mass density, by the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity. Zero matrix trace means no leading change of a small initially resting cloud's volume at order t2, not that each separation stays fixed. Inside matter, the same sign convention gives trT=−4πGρ instead.

Subtracting the constant and uniform-acceleration terms from the point-mass relative potential gives ψtid​=Gmp​[3(r⋅rp​)2−r2]/(2rp3​), with force convention ∇ψ. Its tidal tensor is Gmp​(3rp​rpT​−I)/rp3​. This is the leading term for target size small compared with separation.

Tidal disruption

Words: 69
Tidal tensor OurBigBook.com
Disruption of a self-gravitating body when differential gravitational acceleration across it exceeds its binding acceleration. For a body of radius R, mass m at distance r from a much more massive body M, the competing scales are GMR/r3 and Gm/R2; their equality gives r∼R(M/m)1/3, up to geometry and internal-structure factors. The tidal tensor gives the directional differential acceleration. A tidal disruption event near a black hole is a specific astronomical application.

Tidal force

Words: 960 Articles: 9
Tidal tensor OurBigBook.com
Differential gravitational acceleration, multiplied by the affected mass, across a spatially extended body. In the linear approximation the acceleration difference is TΔr, where T is the tidal tensor. Stellar tidal forces limit the domain of a circumplanetary orbit; sufficiently strong ones can produce tidal disruption.
To isolate a tidal force, subtract the gravitational acceleration shared by the body as a whole. Let a reference test particle follow R¨=g(R), and let another have position R+x. In a translating accelerated reference frame with parallel, nonrotating axes,
x¨=g(R+x)−g(R)=T(R)x+O(R4μ∣x∣2​)
(15)
for a source point mass, when ∣x∣/R≪1. Here μ=GM is its standard gravitational parameter and the last term uses Big O notation. The gravitational constant G sets the strength of Newton's law of universal gravitation. Two point masses M and m a center-to-center distance r apart attract with force magnitude

For bodies with spherical symmetry, the same exterior formula follows from the spherical shell theorem; for arbitrary extended bodies, add the attractions of their mass density elements instead. The gravitational constant connects a laboratory attraction to the Newtonian gravitational field controlling a Kepler orbit.
The gravitational constant G and local gravitational acceleration g are different quantities. Applying Newton's second law to a test particle gives g=F/m=GM/r2 for one spherical source. The source's mass and the observer's position change g; G remains the same parameter of the law. A local falling-body experiment therefore measures a field, not G alone. On rotating Earth, an instrument fixed to the surface also responds to centrifugal acceleration, while surrounding mass density and altitude change the gravitational contribution.
Dimensional analysis explains the units. Denote the base physical dimensions of length, mass and time by L,M,T. Since force has dimension MLT−2,

G=6.67430(15)×10−11m3kg−1s−2

for the 2022 CODATA adjustment, the latest adjustment listed when checked on 14 October 2026. The adjustment year is 2022; NIST's May 2024 data update is a different date.[ref] [ref]

The corresponding acceleration of either mass is 6.67430×10−11ms−2 at that instant. Reducing the separation to 0.10m multiplies both by 100. These are ideal model predictions, not observations; their tiny scale explains why stray forces matter.
Being a constant of a physical law does not make the numerical value exact. The SI fixes the numerical values of seven defining constants, including the speed of light and Planck constant; G is determined experimentally. Exact unit definitions still require physical realizations with measurement uncertainty: calibrating a length or a mass does not become error-free.[ref]

Source positioning, mass density variation and cloud geometry limited the reported combined relative standard uncertainty to 150 parts per million.[ref]

Measuring wave phase accurately is one part of the task; calculating K accurately is another. It is the free-space Green function of the Laplacian with the normalization of the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity. Differentiating gives inward gravitational acceleration −GM/r2. With z=r/r0​, the normalized Newtonian gravitational potential is Φ/(GM/r0​)=−1/z; at z=1,2,4 it equals −1,−1/2,−1/4.
For a radially outward launch from r0​, conservation of mechanical energy in the fixed-source test particle approximation gives the minimum escape velocity:
mE​=2v02​​−r0​GM​=0⟹vesc​=r0​2GM​​.
(38)
At this threshold the speed tends to zero only at infinite separation. The model neglects air resistance, external tidal forces, and general relativity. [ref]
A circular orbit at r0​ instead requires tangential speed vc​=GM/r0​​. Choosing units with G=M=r0​=1 gives g0​=1, vc​=1, and vesc​=2​≃1.41421. A radial launch at speed 1 reaches r=2 and returns; the same speed directed tangentially gives a circular orbit. [ref]
Self-gravity in a thin spherical shell expansion (Wself​=−GMs2​/(2R))
Words: 47
Newtonian potential of a point mass OurBigBook.com
A shell of fixed mass Ms​ and radius R has self-energy −GMs2​/(2R). Its inward generalized force opposing an increase of radius is GMs2​/(2R2). Including this in a swept-gas shell threshold changes an interior-only factor f(1−f) to f(1−f/2) when the original total mass is held fixed.
Gravitational potential of a truncated inverse-radius sphere (Φ(r)=−k′(2r0​−r))
Words: 32
Newtonian potential of a point mass OurBigBook.com
The sphere ρ=k′/(2πGr) for r<r0​ has M(r)=k′r2/G and Φ(r)=−k′(2r0​−r), with zero potential at infinity. Its finite central potential contrasts with the logarithmic central divergence of a truncated inverse-square density.
Axisymmetric gravitational potential of a displaced cylindrical interface (ψin​=−4πGρRK0​(kR)I0​(kr)η)
Words: 83
Newtonian potential of a point mass OurBigBook.com
Consider a uniform-density cylinder with an axisymmetric radial Fourier mode η=ϵeikz. Its displaced boundary gives a first-order surface mass density ρη, although the interior density perturbation vanishes. The gravitational Poisson equation reduces to Laplace equation away from the interface. Regularity internally and decay externally give ψin​=AI0​(kr)eikz and ψout​=BK0​(kr)eikz. Continuity at R and the derivative jump ψout′​−ψin′​=4πGρϵeikz, together with I0​(κ)K0′​(κ)−I0′​(κ)K0​(κ)=−1/κ, give the title amplitude. The prime differentiates the modified Bessel function argument. This axial mode is different from an azimuthal mode on a gravitational potential of a displaced cylindrical interface.

Spherically symmetric potential

Words: 21
Newtonian gravitational potential OurBigBook.com
A spherically symmetric potential depends only on distance r from one point. Its force is central, so angular momentum is conserved.

Newtonian gravitational potential energy

Words: 150 Articles: 3
Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
Two point masses m1​,m2​ separated by distance r have potential energy
V(r)=−rGm1​m2​​.
(39)
The corresponding attractive force is −∇V.
This is the Newtonian point-mass specialization of gravitational energy, with the reference value chosen at infinite separation.

Spherical binding-energy mass integral (W=−2G​∫0∞​M(r)2r−2dr)

Words: 42
Newtonian gravitational potential energy OurBigBook.com
Assembling a spherical mass distribution in shells gives gravitational potential energy W=−G∫M(r)dM(r)/r. Integration by parts gives the displayed identity when M(r)2/r vanishes at both endpoints. It includes each interacting pair once; no extra factor of one half belongs in the original shell-assembly integral.

Minimum-separation binding-energy bounds (B0​≤rU≤A0​)

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Newtonian gravitational potential energy OurBigBook.com
For positive masses, let r be the actual minimum pairwise separation and use positive binding energy U=∑j<k​Gmj​mk​/rjk​. If m(1)​,m(2)​ are the smallest masses, then Gm(1)​m(2)​≤rU≤G∑j<k​mj​mk​. Thus U−1 is comparable to r with constants depending only on the masses.
Negative-energy minimum-separation upper bound (r≤A0​/∣E∣)
Words: 33
Minimum-separation binding-energy bounds OurBigBook.com
With E=T−U<0 and T≥0, the positive binding energy satisfies U≥∣E∣. The minimum-separation binding-energy bounds imply r≤A0​/∣E∣. At least one pair stays close; this does not bound every particle's distance or exclude a negative-energy gravitational collision.

Cavendish experiment

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Newtonian gravitational field OurBigBook.com
The Cavendish experiment makes the attraction predicted by Newton's law of universal gravitation measurable between laboratory masses. Two small test masses hang at the ends of a horizontal rod in a Cavendish torsion balance; nearby larger source masses exert a tiny torque. A thin suspension fiber supplies an opposing torque as it twists. Measuring its twist and calibrating its torsion constant lets an experimenter infer the gravitational force and, in a modern analysis, the gravitational constant. [ref]
The beautiful feature is that the two horizontal forces can cancel as vectors while their torques add. The instrument converts weak attraction into a rotation, with sensitivity set by the fiber's torsion constant. Earth's much larger downward gravitational weight is supported by the suspension rather than supplying the intended torque about its vertical axis. A laboratory measurement can therefore probe the same Newtonian gravitational field that governs the two-body problem.
Henry Cavendish's original paper was Experiments to determine the Density of the Earth, published in Philosophical Transactions, volume 88 (1798), pp. 469–526, and read on 21 June 1798. On p. 469 he credits John Michell with the apparatus idea and explains that Michell died before using it; the instrument reached Cavendish through Francis John Hyde Wollaston. Cavendish's stated aim was Earth's mean mass density. Calling the experiment a determination of the gravitational constant is a modern interpretation, not Cavendish's own formulation of his result. [ref]
The connection between Earth's mean mass density and the gravitational constant follows in a spherical, nonrotating model of Earth. With Earth mass ME​, radius RE​, and surface gravitational acceleration g, the spherical shell theorem and Newton's law of universal gravitation give
g=RE2​GME​​,ρ​E​=4πRE3​3ME​​,G=4πRE​ρ​E​3g​.
(40)
Thus a local comparison of gravitational attractions, together with knowledge of Earth's size and surface gravitational acceleration, reaches a property of the entire planet. These are modern equations explaining the connection, not equations quoted from Cavendish's paper.
For a worked example, use an explicitly simplified two-near-pair model. Each test point mass is m, each source point mass is M, and each lever arm is L, so the rod's full length is 2L. Neglect the rod's mass. At zero twist put the test masses at (−L,0) and (L,0), and the sources at (−L,−r) and (L,r). Here r is the near-pair center separation. Ignore each source's attraction on the test mass at the opposite end. Evaluate the two near-pair forces at zero twist and treat their torque as constant for a small twist, requiring L∣θ∣≪r. This is a teaching model, not a precision model of Cavendish's actual apparatus.
By Newton's law of universal gravitation, each retained force has magnitude F=GmM/r2. The left force points down and the right force points up. Using torque about the suspension axis, both contributions are counterclockwise when viewed from above:
τz,left​=(−L)(−F)=LF,τz,right​=LF,∣τg​∣=2Lr2GmM​.
(41)
The net retained horizontal force is zero, yet the net torque is positive. Moving the sources to (−L,r) and (L,−r) reverses both forces and hence the torque. In a real apparatus, the opposite source also attracts each test mass; that correction is explicitly included in the university derivation. [ref]
For illustrative parameters, take m=0.010kg, M=1.0kg, r=0.050m, L=0.10m, and torsion constant κ=1.0×10−8Nm/rad. Use G=6.67430×10−11m3kg−1s−2, the central value in NIST's 2022 CODATA table; that table gives standard uncertainty 0.00015×10−11m3kg−1s−2. This is an input for the example, not a measurement made with these assumed parameters. [ref]
F=(0.050)2(6.67430×10−11)(0.010)(1.0)​=2.66972×10−10N,∣τg​∣=2(0.10)F=5.33944×10−11Nm.
(42)
This sub-nanonewton force produces a measurable twist in the Cavendish torsion balance. The displayed digits make the toy calculation reproducible; they do not describe experimental precision.

Cavendish torsion balance

Words: 585
Cavendish experiment OurBigBook.com
A Cavendish torsion balance is a torsion balance arranged to measure gravitational torque from nearby source masses. Its suspended horizontal rod rotates about a vertical fiber. In the linear elastic regime, a twist angle θ, measured from the fiber's untwisted orientation, gives a restoring torque τfiber​=−κθ, where κ>0 is the torsion constant. The minus sign is essential: the fiber resists the twist. Under an approximately constant gravitational torque, the rotational equation using moment of inertia I and angular acceleration θ¨ is
Iθ¨=τg​−κθ,θeq​=κτg​​.
(43)
At equilibrium, the two torques balance. The angle is a displacement from the fiber's reference orientation, not the largest excursion during an oscillation. [ref]
For the toy parameters in the Cavendish experiment, the predicted equilibrium twist is
θeq​=1.0×10−85.33944×10−11​=0.00533944rad≃0.3059∘.
(44)
Here L∣θeq​∣/r≃0.0107, consistent with using a small geometric displacement in the toy model, but not an estimate of its total measurement error. Reversing the source positions ideally takes the equilibrium angle from +θeq​ to −θeq​: the magnitude of the change is 2∣θeq​∣≃0.6119∘. A stable zero offset then cancels in the difference. A real reading may track a reflected light spot; the law of reflection doubles a mirror's rotation in the outgoing beam, so the spot's angular change must not be confused with the rod's angle. [ref]
How can the fiber's torsion constant be found without already knowing the gravitational force? Measure the oscillation period and calculate the moment of inertia. For the same toy rod, neglecting its mass and treating both test masses as point masses, I=mL2+mL2=2mL2. With the source torque absent or treated as constant, let ϕ=θ−θeq​ be a small departure from equilibrium. Neglect damping and any change of gravitational torque with angle. The rotational equation becomes simple harmonic motion:
Iϕ¨​+κϕ=0,ϕ(t)=Acos(ωt+δ),ω=Iκ​​,T=2πκI​​,κ=T24π2I​.
(45)
Here A is the angular amplitude, δ specifies the initial phase, and ω is the angular frequency. A softer fiber gives a larger equilibrium twist but also a longer oscillation period: greater sensitivity costs observation time. An undamped oscillation does not settle at equilibrium; damping is needed for settling. [ref]
The toy moment of inertia and undamped oscillation period are
I=2(0.010)(0.10)2=2.0×10−4kgm2,T=2π1.0×10−82.0×10−4​​≃888.5766s≃14.81min.
(46)
Timing this oscillation period would recover the assumed torsion constant. The units check explains the result: torque divided by torsion constant is an angle in radians, and I/κ has units of time squared when radians are treated as dimensionless in SI.
Combining the equilibrium twist with the period calibration, the two-near-pair model would infer the gravitational constant as
G=2LmMκ∣θeq​∣r2​=MT24π2Lr2∣θeq​∣​.
(47)
The test mass cancels in the second expression because it enters both the gravitational torque and the toy moment of inertia. If the measured quantity is the magnitude ∣Δθ∣ of the change between opposite source positions, use ∣θeq​∣=∣Δθ∣/2. Substituting the toy twist and oscillation period returns the input G; it is a consistency check, not independent experimental evidence.
The sensitivity of a Cavendish torsion balance also explains its practical difficulty. Air motion can exert unwanted torque; unequal temperatures can drive that motion. Cavendish discusses this effect on p. 471 and describes observing from outside a closed room to avoid disturbing the instrument. [ref] Mechanical vibrations can excite the same slow oscillations used to calibrate the torsion constant, while changes in the fiber or source separations alter the inferred force. Precision therefore depends on resolving the equilibrium angle, calibrating the full suspended moment of inertia and torsion constant, and modeling the actual source geometry. The two-near-pair model omits opposite-source attraction, rod contributions, finite-size effects, damping, and the variation of gravitational torque as the rod turns. [ref]
